script.opening: "The outside of my right elbow’s been sore for a few weeks now — it really hurts when I grip things, lift the kettle, or even shake hands. I didn’t injure it; it just came on. I do a lot of repetitive work with my hands. What is it, and will it settle?"

facts.text: Right (dominant) elbow, about 8 weeks. Points on camera to the bony bit on the outside of the elbow; sometimes aches down the back of the forearm. Worse gripping, lifting the kettle, turning a screwdriver, shaking hands.

Presses the outer bony point himself: "Ow — that’s it." Holding his arm straight, palm down, and lifting the back of his hand against his other hand: "That hurts right on the spot." Full elbow bending and straightening. Can lift and spread his fingers normally.
No injury. No neck pain, no tingling or numbness in the hand, no weakness lifting the fingers. Elbow not hot, red or swollen. No fever. No other joints affected, no morning stiffness, no psoriasis.
Plasterer — self-employed. Uses a trowel and hawk all day. Busy period; worried about losing income. Does not play racquet sports.
Fit and well. "Nothing much" — the odd paracetamol. No stomach ulcers, no asthma, no kidney problems. No allergies.

Practical, a bit impatient. Ask "How long will it take?" and "What about an injection? I’ve heard about those — my mate had one." Accept the explanation that injections may make it worse in the long run, and that you’d "rather do it properly". Interested in a strap.

ice.concerns: "How long it’ll last and whether I can keep working — I don’t get sick pay."
ice.expectations: "A steroid injection, like my mate had, to get me back to work."

checkpoints.text: Recognises LATERAL EPICONDYLITIS (tennis elbow) — lateral elbow pain, tender lateral epicondyle, pain on gripping and resisted wrist/finger extension, from repetitive use without acute injury

Distinguishes it from medial epicondylitis, radial tunnel syndrome/posterior interosseous nerve entrapment (finger-drop weakness), referred cervical/neuro pain, elbow OA and septic/inflammatory arthritis — checking the neck and elbow by guided self-examination on video, with an in-person examination if any doubt — recognising imaging is not routinely needed

Manages conservatively — load management/activity modification without complete rest, topical NSAIDs (up to about 4 weeks), a forearm strap (may not help), and physiotherapy with progressive ECCENTRIC strengthening — with ergonomic advice (BESS 2023)
Explains that corticosteroid injection is NOT recommended (short-term relief but poorer outcomes and more recurrence at a year, Coombes 2013; BESS 2023) and refers for refractory cases

Sets realistic expectations about the slow but favourable (months; about 9 in 10 improve within a year) course, acknowledges the impact on grip/work, and checks understanding of the exercise/brace plan

Acknowledges the impact on his manual work and everyday grip tasks, and explores what he needs to keep doing, tailoring the load-management advice to his job and offering a fit note for amended duties if needed
Negotiates a realistic self-management plan (brace and progressive exercises), gives clear explained instructions, and checks he is confident to carry it out

Safety-nets and follows up: review if not improving, escalate (physio/orthopaedics) if refractory, and reconsider for atypical/neurological features (numbness, weakness, finger drop, hot swollen elbow, fever) — conservative-first management

worked.txt: "This is tennis elbow — an overuse strain of the tendons on the outer elbow where they attach to the bone. The repetitive gripping work has set it off, and that’s why gripping and shaking hands hurt. It’s not serious and it does settle."
"I’ll be upfront — it can be slow, often a few months, but around nine in ten people have improved within a year, exercises help it along, and we don’t usually need scans."

"The mainstays are easing the aggravating gripping where you can without resting it completely, an anti-inflammatory gel for the first few weeks, a forearm strap if it helps you (it doesn’t for everyone), and — most importantly — physiotherapy with specific strengthening exercises that actually help the tendon heal. I’ll refer you for those."
"A steroid injection can ease it for a few weeks, but studies show people who have one are less likely to have recovered at a year and more likely to have it come back — so I don’t recommend it."

"Let’s look at your work technique and tools too, since that’s the driver — small changes reduce the strain, like lifting palm-up and using thicker handles. If work is hard to manage, I can give you a fit note suggesting adjusted duties."

"Come back if it’s not improving with the exercises and brace, or if you get pins and needles, neck symptoms, weakness or trouble straightening your fingers, or a hot swollen elbow or fever — that would make me think again. Otherwise, patience and the exercises will get you there."

f.learning: LATERAL EPICONDYLITIS (tennis elbow) is an overuse TENDINOPATHY of the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle, recognised by lateral elbow pain with local tenderness, worse on GRIPPING/lifting and resisted wrist/finger EXTENSION (e.g. positive Cozen’s test), typically from repetitive forearm use and coming on without acute injury. Distinguish it from medial epicondylitis (golfer’s elbow), radial tunnel syndrome (more distal, no point epicondyle tenderness), referred cervical/neurological pain (neck symptoms, paraesthesiae) and elbow osteoarthritis (older, stiffness/crepitus) — clinical features usually suffice and imaging is not routinely needed. Finger-drop weakness suggests posterior interosseous nerve entrapment and is urgent; a hot swollen joint suggests septic or inflammatory arthritis. Manage conservatively, as it is largely self-limiting over months (about 89% improve within a year without active treatment, Ikonen 2022): load management/activity modification without complete rest (reduce aggravating gripping), topical NSAIDs for up to about 4 weeks, a forearm (counterforce) strap that may be offered but may not help, and physiotherapy with progressive ECCENTRIC strengthening exercises, plus ergonomic advice on tools and technique and a fit note for amended duties where needed — these are first-line (BESS pathway, Singh 2023). A corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but worse outcomes at a year (recovery 83% vs 96% with placebo, recurrence 54% vs 12%, Coombes, JAMA 2013), so BESS advises against it; refer to MSK/orthopaedic services for refractory cases after several months of well-done exercise-based care (shockwave only with special arrangements, NICE HTG201). Set realistic, slow-recovery expectations, reassure about the favourable course, and safety-net for atypical/neurological features that would prompt reconsideration.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BESS patient care pathway: tennis elbow, Singh et al., Shoulder Elbow 2023 · [2] Coombes et al., JAMA 2013 · [3] Smidt et al., Lancet 2002 · [4] Ikonen et al., Clin Orthop Relat Res 2022 · [5] NICE HTG201 Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for refractory tennis elbow (2009) · [6] NICE HTG299 Autologous blood injection for tendinopathy (2013)
knowledge.summary: Lateral elbow pain after repetitive gripping, with tenderness at the lateral epicondyle and pain on resisted wrist extension, is tennis elbow (lateral elbow tendinopathy). It is a clinical diagnosis and imaging is not needed. Most people improve within a year. Explain the natural history, adjust load at work and home without stopping activity, and use progressive loading exercises through physiotherapy. Topical NSAIDs help short-term; a strap may help some. Corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief but worse outcomes at a year and more recurrence, and BESS advises against it. Reassess for neck, nerve or joint causes if atypical.

points.t: Pain and tenderness at or just distal to the lateral epicondyle, reproduced by gripping and resisted wrist or middle-finger extension. History and examination (on video the patient can show the tender point and resisted wrist extension against their other hand) are enough; plain X-ray only if the diagnosis is uncertain, for example suspected fracture, arthritis or loose bodies [1]. Peak age is 45–54.

Cervical radiculopathy (neck pain, arm paraesthesia, reflex or myotomal change), radial tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve entrapment (tenderness distal to the epicondyle; finger-drop weakness is urgent), elbow osteoarthritis or loose bodies (stiffness, locking), and inflammatory or septic arthritis (hot, swollen joint).

In trials, about 89% of people given no active treatment reported improvement within the first year [4]. Wait-and-see achieved success in 83% at 52 weeks [3]. Recurrence is more likely with symptoms beyond 12 months, acute pain at onset, previous steroid injection and poor adherence [1].

Education and load adjustment: reduce provoking gripping and lifting (palm-up lifting, thicker tool handles, spreading tasks) without complete rest. Physiotherapy with progressive extensor loading and stretching is strongly recommended [1]. A counterforce strap may be offered but may not help [1]. Topical NSAIDs relieve pain for up to about 4 weeks; oral NSAID evidence is conflicting; check risk and dose per BNF.

Corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief but worse longer-term outcomes. At one year, recovery was 83% with injection against 96% with placebo, and recurrence 54% against 12% [2]. Against physiotherapy, success at 52 weeks was 69% with injection versus 91% [3]. BESS advises against steroid injection and against autologous blood injection [1,6].

If disabling symptoms persist after several months of well-done exercise-based care, review the diagnosis and refer to MSK or orthopaedic services. Shockwave therapy is available only with special arrangements for governance, consent and audit (NICE HTG201 [5]). Surgery is a secondary-care decision for a small minority.

model.text: Hello Mr Holloway, I’m Dr Shah. What’s brought you in?

The outside of my right elbow’s been sore for a few weeks now. It really hurts when I grip things, lift the kettle, or even shake hands. I didn’t injure it; it just came on. I do a lot of repetitive work with my hands. What is it, and will it settle?
Thanks, that’s a helpful description. I’ll ask a few questions and ask you to do a few movements on the camera, and then we’ll talk about what it is and how to get it better.
Can you point to where it hurts most? Does the pain spread anywhere?
Just here on the outside bony bit. Sometimes a bit down the forearm.
Tell me about your work. What movements do you do most, and how is it coping?
A lot of gripping and repetitive movements. It’s getting harder to do my job properly.
Any neck pain, or pins and needles, numbness or weakness in the arm or hand? Any trouble straightening your fingers?
model.why: Cervical radiculopathy and posterior interosseous nerve screen

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Does the elbow swell, lock or catch, or get stiff so you can’t straighten it? Any fevers, or feeling unwell?
model.why: Joint pathology, loose bodies, septic arthritis

model.text: No. It’s just sore.
Any other joints painful or swollen, back stiffness in the mornings, or skin rashes like psoriasis?
No.
What have you taken for it so far? Any stomach, kidney or heart problems?
Nothing much. No problems like that.

Can you turn your head side to side, then bend and straighten both elbows for me? … Your neck moves freely without bringing on arm symptoms, and the elbow looks normal and moves fully. Press on the outer bony point — is that the spot? And if you push the back of your right hand up against your left hand, does that bring it on? … That fits. Your grip is painful but you say it’s strong, and you’ve no numbness or weakness in the arm.
model.why: Neck, elbow and resisted extension on video; neurological symptoms screened

model.text: What did you think it might be? And what worries you most?
I thought it was the work. I’m worried about how long it’ll last and whether I can keep working.

You’re right that the work has a lot to do with it. This is tennis elbow: the tendons that pull your wrist back attach to that bony point, and repeated gripping has overloaded them. It’s not serious and you don’t need an X-ray.
model.why: Names diagnosis; links to load; no imaging

model.text: How long will it take?
Honestly, it can be slow. It usually takes months rather than weeks, but around nine in ten people have improved within a year, and exercises can help it along.

The key is managing the load, not resting it completely. Where you can, grip less tightly, lift with your palm facing up, use thicker handles, and break up repetitive tasks. I’ll refer you to physio for a programme of gradually strengthening exercises, which is the most helpful treatment.
model.why: Load adjustment and physiotherapy loading programme

model.text: An anti-inflammatory gel can ease the pain for the first few weeks. Some people find a forearm strap helps, though it doesn’t work for everyone.
model.why: Topical NSAID and strap, with honest caveats

model.text: What about an injection? I’ve heard about those.
A steroid injection can ease the pain for a few weeks, but studies show people who have one are less likely to have recovered at a year and more likely to have it come back. So I don’t recommend it.
Right. I’d rather do it properly then.
If work is hard to manage, I can give you a fit note suggesting adjusted duties, so you can keep working while it recovers.
model.why: Addresses work concern; fit note for amended duties

model.text: That might help, yes.

Come back sooner if you get numbness, pins and needles or weakness, trouble straightening your fingers, a hot swollen elbow or fever. Otherwise, if it isn’t improving after a few months of the exercises, we’ll review and think about a specialist opinion. Can you tell me the plan?
Ease the gripping, physio exercises, gel for now, maybe a strap, no injection, a fit note if I need it, and back if I get numbness or weakness or it’s not improving.
Perfect. The physio referral will go today.

social.t: Repetitive gripping drives symptoms. Task rotation, tool changes and pacing reduce load while he keeps working.
Lifting kettles and shopping bags palm-up, and using both hands, reduce strain.

legal.t: A fit note can say he may be fit for work with amended duties or workplace adaptations, rather than signing him off.

professional.t: Explaining why a requested injection is not recommended, with figures, supports shared decision-making.
Routine imaging and steroid injection add cost and harm in a typical case.

community.t: Many areas offer self-referral to MSK physiotherapy; occupational health may help with workplace adjustments.

redFlags: Finger-drop or wrist-drop weakness: posterior interosseous or radial nerve lesion, urgent
Neck pain with arm paraesthesia or weakness: cervical radiculopathy
Hot, swollen elbow or fever: septic arthritis
Locking or loss of extension: loose body or arthritis
Unexplained bone pain or growing lump: sarcoma pathways
ice: Concern: how long; whether he can keep working

pitfalls.intro: A common, clinically obvious diagnosis. Marks go to excluding neck and nerve causes, giving evidence-based advice on load and exercise, handling the injection question, and supporting him at work.

items.fail: Not assessing the neck and nerves.
items.why: Cervical radiculopathy and nerve entrapment mimic tennis elbow.
items.fix: Screen neck movement, power, sensation and reflexes.

items.why: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging only if uncertain.

legal.t: A fit note can say he may be fit for work with amended duties or workplace adaptations, rather than signing him off.

professional.t: Explaining why a requested injection is not recommended, with figures, supports shared decision-making.
Routine imaging and steroid injection add cost and harm in a typical case.

community.t: Many areas offer self-referral to MSK physiotherapy; occupational health may help with workplace adjustments.

redFlags: Finger-drop or wrist-drop weakness: posterior interosseous or radial nerve lesion, urgent
Neck pain with arm paraesthesia or weakness: cervical radiculopathy
Hot, swollen elbow or fever: septic arthritis
Locking or loss of extension: loose body or arthritis
Unexplained bone pain or growing lump: sarcoma pathways
ice: Concern: how long; whether he can keep working

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is tennis elbow: the tendons on the outside of the elbow are overloaded where they attach to the bone.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a rope tied to a post. Pull on it thousands of times a day and it starts to fray where it’s tied. Rest alone doesn’t strengthen it, but building up the load gradually does.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried about how long it would take and about work. Most people get better within a year, and we can adjust your duties so you can keep working.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him working with adjusted tasks; offer a fit note if needed.
sharedPlan: Load adjustment at work and home
Topical NSAID for up to about 4 weeks; strap optional
safetyNet: Numbness, weakness or finger-drop, hot swollen elbow or fever: urgent review
Not improving after several months of exercise: review and consider referral

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: A common, clinically obvious diagnosis. Marks go to excluding neck and nerve causes, giving evidence-based advice on load and exercise, handling the injection question, and supporting him at work.

items.fail: Not assessing the neck and nerves.
items.why: Cervical radiculopathy and nerve entrapment mimic tennis elbow.
items.fix: Screen neck movement, power, sensation and reflexes.

items.why: Diagnosis is clinical; imaging only if uncertain.
Worse outcomes and more recurrence at one year.
items.fix: Explain the evidence and recommend loading exercises.

items.why: Progressive loading is the effective treatment.
items.fix: Adjust load and refer to physiotherapy.

items.why: Work drives symptoms and his main worry is his job.
items.fix: Tailor advice; offer a fit note for amended duties.
Give honest figures and a review plan.
